plan.topic_summary: Backside power delivery (BSPDN) is a silicon process architecture that relocates the power delivery network to the backside of the die, freeing frontside area for transistors. It matters for a 1–5 year view because it is a prerequisite for continued transistor density scaling at leading-edge nodes and will reshape equipment, packaging, and thermal design across the semiconductor supply chain.
key_questions: Which leading-edge process nodes have BSPDN in volume production and what are the reported yield and cost impacts over the next 12 months?
How does BSPDN affect thermal management and packaging requirements for high-power chips over the next 1–3 years?
What are the known reliability and defect mechanisms specific to backside power vias, and how do they compare to frontside power delivery at equivalent current densities?
How does BSPDN interact with advanced packaging approaches such as chiplet interposers and 3D stacking over a 3–5 year horizon?
What equipment and process steps are unique to BSPDN, and what are the supply-chain concentration risks for those steps?

sources.title: Leading Edge Technologies: Backside Power Delivery
sources.abstract: Abstract An architectural shift to buried power rails (BPRs) with backside power delivery (BPD) is on the horizon as CMOS technology approaches the 2 nm node. The obstruction created by the presence of BPD networks obsoletes many of the electrical fault isolation (EFI) techniques that have been used for the past few decades and severely degrades the performance of others. This chapter provides an overview of EFI methods that are still applicable to ICs with BPD networks, including e-beam and atomic force probing, x-ray and magnetic field imaging, and lock-in thermography. It assesses the technical challenges of each method as well as the potential for improvement.

sources.title: CSCO: A Backside-PDN-Aware Clock-Signal Co-Optimization Framework for Improved PPA
sources.abstract: Backside power delivery networks (BSPDN) have emerged as a promising technology for advanced logic nodes to address IR-drop and PPA challenges. While BSPDN introduces additional routing resources on the backside, these resources are limited and must be carefully partitioned between clock and signal nets, creating a critical resource allocation tradeoff. Prior work either moves only the clock network or assumes a fixed clock tree and optimizes only signal nets, failing to explore the tradeoff space of backside resource allocation. Moreover, lacking frontside power-ground shielding, BSPDN introduces severe signal integrity (SI) degradation. We propose CSCO, a data-driven BSPDN-aware co-optimization framework that jointly allocates limited backside resources between clock and signal nets across frontside/backside layers. CSCO employs efficient search strategies to identify critical nets for backside routing without repeated evaluation, navigating the clock-signal allocation tradeoff to balance IR-drop, routing congestion, and PPA. The framework also leverages backside routing to mitigate coupling noise and crosstalk-induced SI issues. Experiments demonstrate improved WNS/TNS, frequency, and SI robustness without additional shielding overhead.

sources.title: Intel PowerVia Technology: Backside Power Delivery for High Density and High-Performance Computing
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: This paper presents a high-yielding backside power delivery (BPD) technology, PowerVia, implemented on Intel 4 finFET process. PowerVia more directly integrates power delivery to the transistor as compared to published buried power rail schemes, enabling additional wiring resources on front side for signal routing. A fabricated E-core with $\gt 90$% cell utilization showed $\gt 30$% platform voltage droop improvement and 6% frequency benefit compared to a similar design without PowerVia. Transistor performance, reliability, and fault isolation capability is detailed.

sources.title: Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology
sources.abstract: Clock meshes are used in high-performance VLSI designs to minimize skew and tolerate on-chip variation, but they spend scarce routing resources on premium metal layers. Backside power delivery creates a new option: it adds thick, low-resistance metal layers on the back of the wafer, and the power grid does not consume all of them. Flip-flops remain on the frontside; a backside mesh therefore cannot drive them directly, and every connection passes through a through-silicon via. We present the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes, implemented in OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology. Four benchmarks (1,938 to 15,311 flip-flops) are explored with multi-objective Bayesian optimization, and every design point is verified by transistor-level SPICE simulation, since the cyclic mesh cannot be evaluated by static timing analysis. Across all four designs, the backside mesh consistently outperforms an identical frontside mesh, with on average 45% lower skew, 25% lower sink slew, 4.5% lower power, and 28% less frontside clock wiring, and its skew spread under 10,000-sample Monte Carlo is a third of the frontside mesh's.

sources.title: Transient Multiscale Workflow for Thermal Analysis of 3DHI Chip Stack
sources.abstract: Modern package designs make use of technologies such as backside power delivery (BSPD) and 3D stacked chiplets that require accounting for the heterogeneity in back end of the line (BEOL) structures in hot-spot prediction. Multiscale homogenization strategies have been demonstrated to be effective for steady-state simulations, however accurate 3D transient simulations that include BEOL structures remain an open challenge. In this work, we demonstrate a transient thermal workflow that accounts for the 3D heterogeneous structures in the BEOL for problems with strong- and weak- temporal scale separation under the assumption of temperature independent constitutive properties. Our workflow, based on Bloomfield et. al. 2025, automatically extracts, meshes, and homogenizes thermal properties from GDSII and OASIS files to construct thermal property maps. Property maps (heat capacity and conductivity) have been generated for a 1 mm by 1 mm SoC-style model die that was constructed with LibreLane for 100 by 100 grids with 5 micron by 5 micron representative volume elements (RVEs), and 50 by 50 grids with 10 micron by 10 micron RVEs. The expressions for a transient effective conductivity are provided and a demonstration of the impact of the transient effects are provided for a single RVE. Finally, transient conductivity maps have been provided for a time integration timestep of dt=0.001.

sources.title: Thermal Impacts of Backside Power Delivery Networks on GAAFET Technology
sources.abstract: The emerging backside power delivery network (BSPDN) technology offers significant advantages in area scaling, IR drop reduction, and operating frequency enhancement. In this work, we systematically investigate the thermal dissipation mechanisms associated with various BSPDN architectures and develop SPICE-compatible dynamic thermal models to facilitate model-driven evaluation for electrical and thermal dynamics at the device-circuit level. A comprehensive evaluation, coupled with the previously developed parasitic model, reveals that the parasitic effects dominate circuit dynamic performance compared to self-heating effects (SHEs), while the SHE exacerbates device degradation mechanisms, such as hot carrier injection (HCI) and bias temperature instability (BTI). Evaluation results indicate that backside contacts (BSCs) are more capable of suppressing SHEs and parasitic effects, while through silicon via in middle-of-line (MOL) (TSVM)-based circuits experience pronounced performance degradation, enabling a model-driven tradeoff strategy for circuit optimization in advanced technology.

sources.title: Low Distortion Fusion Bonding using Pneumatically Warped Wafers
sources.venue: 2026 IEEE 76th Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC), Orlando, FL, USA, 2026, pp. 1349-1356
sources.abstract: Backside power-delivery-network (BSPDN) schemes require wafer-to-wafer bonding steps that do not leave high order shape changes or localized stresses in the bonded stack to ensure that these don't get transferred to the thinned wafer for further lithographic exposure. However, bonding mechanics involve strong adhesive forces which can inherently create localized distortions that lithography tools must eventually compensate. Some contributors to grid distortion of the target wafer are, method of bond initiation, bond front velocity variations, and lack of symmetry between the wafers. In this work, we evaluate a low-distortion bonding approach in the SUSS XBA tool, where some of these contributors are tackled at the source, namely by initiating the bond without a localized external force, and keeping the wafers compliant & symmetric during bonding. Wafers are bonded with a slight pre-stress due to controlled gas pressure applied over the whole backside of the wafers throughout bonding. Wafer-shape measurements of the bonded stacks are used to perform gradient-based in-plane-displacements (IPD) modelling to estimate bonding-induced grid distortion. Dense scanner metrology is used on patterned-bonded wafers to confirm the location and severity of distortion predictions from patterned wafer geometry (PWG) measurements. On the PWG distortion maps and scanner grid readouts, we perform alignment and CPE modelling with different field layouts. Sub-10 nm levels of residual grid distortion are achievable with relatively low-order correction models, and less than or equal to 3 nm by using advanced CPE models. These results demonstrate that pneumatically warped bonding yields low-distortion bonded stacks, and that simple process tuning can decouple the dominant distortion source from edge-related variability.

sources.title: Nano-Through Silicon Vias (nTSV) for Backside Power Delivery Networks (BSPDN)
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: In this paper we discuss the driving forces for moving to chip backside power delivery. Possible integration flows and challenges are discussed for integrating through-silicon via (TSV) connections that directly interconnect the chip at the standard-cell level. These approaches use power rail integration schemes that can be “buried” in the STI and Si below the devices or directly integrated as backside metallization scheme on the wafer backside. Both nTSV “last” and “first” integration flows have been demonstrated. Key technology challenges are the extreme wafer thinning required and back-side lithography correction to correct for wafer distortions caused by wafer processing and W2W bonding.

sources.title: Thermal Implications of Non-Uniform Power in BSPDN-Enabled 2.5D/3D Chiplet-based Systems-in-Package using Nanosheet Technology
sources.abstract: Advances in nanosheet technologies have significantly increased power densities, exacerbating thermal management challenges in 2.5D/3D chiplet-based Systems-in-Package (SiP). While traditional thermal analyses often employ uniform power maps to simplify computational complexity, this practice neglects localized heating effects, leading to inaccuracies in thermal estimations, especially when comparing power delivery networks (PDN) in 3D integration. This work examines the thermal impact of non-uniform power distributions on SiPs utilizing frontside (FSPDN) and backside (BSPDN) power delivery approaches. Using high-resolution thermal simulations with non-uniform power maps at resolutions down to 5 micrometers, we demonstrate that uniform power assumptions substantially underestimate peak temperatures and fail to reveal critical thermal differences between BSPDN and FSPDN configurations in 3D scenarios. Our results highlight that BSPDN configurations in 3D, although beneficial in simplified uniform scenarios, exhibit pronounced thermal penalties under realistic, localized workloads due to limited lateral heat spreading. These findings emphasize the necessity of adopting fine-grained, workload-aware power maps in early-stage thermal modeling to enable accurate PDN assessment and informed thermal-aware design decisions in advanced nanosheet-based 3D SiP.

sources.title: Thermal Mitigation Strategy for Backside Power Delivery Network
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: By improving power delivery capability and mitigating signal routing congestion, Back Side Power Delivery Network (BSPDN) has been proven to be a game changer for the next generation of chip design. However, it also brings thermal challenges due to a significantly larger thermal resistance between the CPU power grid and on-chip forced cooling. Therefore, a cutting-edge cooling scheme is needed to tackle this issue. Inspired by the similarity between Back End of Line (BEOL) layer structure and 3D manifolded microchannel cooler, we propose an innovative embedded microchannel cooling configuration to bring the coolant closer to FEOL, which also cooperates with chip-top jet cooling to form a dual-sided cooling system. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) is performed to study the thermal performance of chips and cooling effectiveness and efficiency for microchannel cooling. Due to the high complexity of a detailed BSPDN model, several engineering approaches are utilized to reduce the computing resource requirement. Detailed Back End of Line (BEOL) thermal models are established and investigated for computing its accurate orthotropic thermal conductivity. Then, a local unit cell model including both BSPDN chip and coolant region are simulated through system coupling approach, after which the effective Heat Transfer Coefficients (HTC) are extracted and applied to a 50 μm × 50 μm overall model with power map heat source. A control parameter study is conducted by varying coolant type of water and air, inlet flow velocity, and inlet flow temperature. It turns out that the microchannel cooling with 283K, 0.06m/s water inlet can reduce the maximum temperature by more than 20% or about 20°C for both uniform heat flux and heat map cases, at an expense of 2581 Pa inlet pressure.

sources.title: Modeling of Backside Power Delivery and Thermal Management in Semiconductor Die Packages
sources.venue: I-THERM :/I-THERM - Intersociety Conference on Thermal Phenomena in Electronic Systems
sources.abstract: Modern semiconductor packaging faces the dual challenges of efficiently delivering power to numerous transistors and managing heat to prevent hotspots and potential component failure. Backside power delivery (BSPD) distinguishes itself from conventional power delivery methods by delivering power from the backside of the silicon die, using unused space for thicker power lines and thereby reducing resistance loss. Embedded microfluidic cooling strategies have investigated microchannels in the back side of silicon dies to direct coolant over hotspots, effectively dissipating heat for chip temperature management. We propose a synergistic integration of microfluidic channels with power delivery on the backside of semiconductor dies that can potentially offer optimized space utilization to allow balanced power and thermal performance. However, this requires modeling tools that can accurately capture coupled electrical and thermal responses in 3D while resolving the small feature sizes relative to the overall die size that can lead to computational complexity. To address this challenge, we develop a model that employs a homogenization method that allows for sub-grid resolution of microscale features, as well as the transformation of the fully 3D problem into an equivalent set of connected 2D subproblem. This work demonstrates application of this method to numerically study a silicon die with both a backside power delivery network (BSPDN) and manifold liquid cooling microchannels. 3D transport is represented by considering the energy and mass exchange between multiple 2D layers. The homogenized representation treats the domain as a porous composite material with metallic power lines navigating between the flow channels. Homogenized conservation thermofluidic conservation equations for the porous medium that consider electrical Joule heating are used to construct the numerical model. Representative steady-state cases are studied where the silicon die generates uniform heating with local hotspots. Through these case studies, we reveal the potential application advantages of integrating 3D manifold microchannels for cooling in a BSPDN for high-power operations.

sources.title: Electromigration of Backside Power Delivery Networks for PPA-Reliability Tradeoffs at N2 Node
sources.venue: Technical digest - International Electron Devices Meeting/Technical digest
sources.abstract: Electromigartion (EM) reliability of backside power delivery network (BSPDN) using three kinds of techniques (BPR, TSVM and BSC) is comprehensively investigated by proposed electro-thermal-stress fully coupled EM simulation method. The physical behaviors of metal atom migration, vacancy generation and void nucleation are reproduced to offer the understanding of microscopic void evolutions. The obtained position of EM failure and resistance degradation show a well agreement with the experiments in different metals. By studying the time to failure (TTF) of various BSPDNs connected to power lines (GND, VDD) with alternative metal materials (W, Ru, Mo), valuable insights can be gained to mitigate potential failure risks and enhance the EM reliability of advanced interconnects technology. The tradeoffs of power-performance-area-reliability (PPAR) are predicted in different BSPDNs at N2 node.

sources.title: Cross-Layer Modeling and Simulation for Electrothermal-Reliability With Backside Power Delivery Networks
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of the Electron Devices Society
sources.abstract: Thermal and reliability are important concerns with the back-side power delivery network (BSPDN) technology. For evaluations of the essential reliability characteristics, this work develops an efficient framework that integrates self-heating effects within BSPDN, enabling SPICE-compatible simulations of self-heating coupled reliability degradation at the circuit level. Analysis reveals that the omission of self-heating results in a significant underestimation of degradation by a factor of 2 to 4. Through comprehensive cross-layer modeling of BSPDN technology, the proposed framework enables a detailed investigation of reliability implications across various BSPDN implementations. It is demonstrated that neglecting the coupled effects from self-heating leads to a 15%-25% underestimation of circuit degradations. The results show that the back-side contact (BSC) is more immune to the coupled degradations. Overall, the proposed method supports thermal-and reliability-aware circuit design and enables more accurate power-performance-area-thermal-reliability (PPA-TR) trade-off optimization.

sources.title: Thermo-Mechanical Reliability Analysis and Raman Spectroscopy Characterization of Sub-micron Through Silicon Vias (TSVs) for Backside Power Delivery in 3D Interconnects
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: This study focuses on the fabrication and thermomechanical characterization of Through Silicon Vias (TSV) with diameters spanning 1-4 µm. In terms of TSV fabrication, scallop-free Si etching is achieved by the optimization of the Bosch etching process, and a void-free TSV filling is completed by a combination of electroless plating for seed layer and electroplating for TSV Cu filler. After that, the thermomechanical response of TSVs is stress-imaged via Raman spectroscopy. Thermal stress is developed in the Si after an annealing process at 400°C, which is attributed to the shrinkage of the Cu core as the sample cools down from the annealing temperature to room temperature. The stress profiles of TSVs with different diameters are measured and compared, revealing an equivalent stress level consistently below 100 MPa for all diameters. This lower stress level is attributed to the offset between tensile radial stress and compressive tangential stress. With the pitch fixed for different-sized TSVs, the interaction between adjacent TSVs is reduced for smaller TSVs, leading to a lower stress level and a transformation from single-peak to dual-peak stress distribution.

sources.title: Backside Interconnects for Power Delivery – Design, Manufacturability & Yield
sources.venue: IEEE Electron Devices Technology & Manufacturing Conference (EDTM)
sources.abstract: Backside power delivery (PowerVia) represents an inflection point in interconnect evolution. With the impending transition of PowerVia from development to high-volume-manufacturing (HVM) at Intel, the rest of the silicon industry is racing to deploy the same. This paper describes approaches to implementing backside power delivery & shows transistor performance data from Intel on both FinFET & RibbonFET. Impact of backside power on design, EDA, manufacturing, reliability and other “perceived” challenges is also discussed. Silicon results from an X-86 Intel E-Core test-chip validating PowerVia benefits are detailed.

sources.title: E-Beam Probing: A Revolutionary Solution for Backside Power Delivery Network (PDN) and Backside Power Vias in Advanced Integrated Circuits
sources.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern integrated circuits, particularly those with multiple power domains and high-performance requirements, has necessitated the adoption of backside power delivery networks and backside power vias. These innovations play a crucial role in mitigating power integrity challenges such as voltage drops, power noise, and thermal effects. However, the characterization and debugging of these structures remain significant challenges due to the inaccessibility of internal metal layers when using traditional probing techniques. E-beam probing emerges as a viable solution, offering deep penetration capabilities, high spatial resolution, and non-invasive measurement techniques. Unlike optical probing, which is limited by diffraction constraints and substrate transparency, e-beam probing can penetrate semiconductor materials to directly access buried power network structures [1,4]. This characteristic makes it an invaluable tool for analyzing backside power delivery networks and identifying potential issues that could affect IC performance and reliability. In modern ICs, especially those with multiple power domains or high-performance requirements, the backside PDN is crucial for ensuring stable and efficient power distribution. It typically consists of multiple metal layers dedicated to power distribution, along with through-silicon vias (TSVs) that connect these layers to the power pads on the IC's surface as shown in Figure 1. The backside PDN is designed to minimize power supply noise, voltage drop, and thermal effects. This is particularly important for maintaining signal integrity and preventing performance degradation or failures due to voltage droops or fluctuations. Designing an effective backside PDN involves careful consideration of the IC's power requirements, the distribution of power domains, the layout of power pads, and the physical properties of the IC substrate. Advanced techniques such as power gating, voltage regulation, and on-die decoupling capacitors may be employed to enhance the performance and reliability of the backside PDN. E-beam probing has advantages over optical probing which makes it particularly useful for analyzing the backside power delivery network (PDN) in advanced ICs [2]. E-beam probing can penetrate through the IC substrate to access the internal metal layers and structures, including the backside PDN. This allows direct observation and measurement of the power distribution network without physically altering the IC [3]. The future of IC design and manufacturing will increasingly rely on advanced analytical techniques to ensure power integrity and performance optimization. Backside power delivery networks and backside power vias are instrumental in addressing the power distribution challenges associated with modern high-performance chips, yet their verification and analysis remain difficult using conventional approaches. E-beam probing provides a compelling solution, enabling non-invasive, high-resolution, and high-frequency analysis of complex power delivery structures. We propose Electron-beam probing (EBP) as an emerging and viable alternative, providing much greater spatial resolution than optical probing and applying it to buried power rails with PDN and complex 3D design systems. As this technology continues to be refined and integrated into mainstream semiconductor analysis workflows, it will play a pivotal role in ensuring the reliability and efficiency of next-generation electronic devices. Motivation for E-beam probing – Buried Power Rails with Back-side PDN (Power Vias)

sources.title: Simulation on Microstructural Evolution under Electromigration in Backside Power Delivery Network
sources.venue: International Conference on Electronic Packaging Technology (ICEPT)
sources.abstract: A state-of-art design, so-called backside power delivery network (BS-PDN), has been proposed for future logic scaling enablement. Nevertheless, electromigration (EM) can be a potential risk causing an increase of electric resistance or even an open circuit failure (OCF) inside the BS-PDN. Here, we use a phase field model to investigate the interplay between microstructural evolution and EM damage in the BS-PDNs. One typical configuration of a BS-PDN, which consists of a nano through-silicon-via (n-TSV), a buried power rail (BPR) and a local metal interconnect (LMI), is referenced to construct the model geometry. The areas near the cathode side interface of each component are regarded as the critical regions where most of EM damages develop. The grain structures in the critical regions, the anisotropic grain boundary (GB) mobility and the material choice for BPR are considered as influential factors on EM reliability. Three criteria on the EM reliability can be put forward, amongst which the most important criterion is the material choice for the BPR because the time to the OCF increases significantly in the BS-PDN with Ru-BPR. The other two criteria are the number of GBs intersecting with the BPR-LMI interface and whether or not these GBs are high angle GBs.

sources.title: Backside Power Delivery: Game Changer and Key Enabler of Advanced Logic Scaling and New STCO Opportunities
sources.venue: Technical digest - International Electron Devices Meeting/Technical digest
sources.abstract: We report on devices built with the power delivery network (PDN) moved to the wafer’s backside (BS) for lower IR drop and improved routing efficiency. This concept can be implemented by differentiated schemes, some of which can be combined for 3D stacked structures such as CFET, and with Buried Power Rail (BPR) connected via scaled nTSV to BSM1 used for a first experimental demonstration. Device fabrication starts with frontside (FS) processing, after which the wafers are flipped over, bonded to carrier wafers and continued for the BS flow. Robust extreme wafer thinning has been achieved with a SiGe-Etch Stop Layer (ESL) added early on the FS, without impacting device properties. Optimized post-BS anneal(s) are shown to be effective for VTrecovery (as some depassivation may occur after FS process), yielding improved mobility, DC performance, reliability and noise behavior. A scenario where the device’s source (S) is directly contacted from the BS (BSC-S) offers higher cell’s scalability potential, with stress, contact resistance, thermal (chip vs. transistor level, focus on hotspots) aspects assessed for various configurations. Its intrinsic S/D asymmetric access can also be explored to obtain low IOFFfor small bandgap Ge/SiGe FETs. Further exploration work shows clear benefits for ESD diodes with BS contacts and for clock distribution implemented with (partial) BS routing, paving the way to a truly functional BS and new STCO opportunities.

sources.title: Structural Reliability and Performance Analysis of Backside PDN
sources.venue: IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology and Circuits (VLSI Technology and Circuits)
sources.abstract: One of the innovative packaging solutions for beyond-4nm node, Backside-Power Delivery Network (BS-PDN) is investigated to analyze the chip package interaction (CPI) effects. BS-PDN configuration contains dense mircothrough silicon vias $(\mu$TSVs) and power/ground metal stack on the backside of the silicon die. By employing submodeling simulation, stress concentration of this both-side backend-of-the-line (BEOL) structure is analyzed with the node displacement of packaging-level macro model as the boundary condition. Compared to the conventional front-side BEOL structure of current 4nm node, stress concentration is observed in the last Dx metal next to $\mu$TSV in BS-PDN structure for expecting risks of delamination. In addition, we analyze the estimated oscillation frequency of an inverter ring oscillator (INV RO) built using BS-PDN. Effects on the dimension of $\mu$TSVs, materials applied in $\mu$TSVs, and the barrier metal thickness of $\mu$TSVs to suggest the optimal scenario with respect to the CPI risks and RO performance of BS-PDN.

sources.title: Characterization of Carbon Contained Films at Bonding Interface for the Application of Backside Power Delivery Networks
sources.abstract: Direct Bonding is gaining attention increasingly as a critical process in the advanced 3D architecture like BSPDN. Achieving new structures in advanced nodes requires robust bonding that ensures high bonding strength, low distortion, and high reliability. However, remaining water at the bonding interface, which affects reliability, is difficult to consume at low temperatures with conventional$\text{SiO}_{2}$dielectricfilms. Wafer to wafer bonding was performed and the bonding interface was evaluated by using a newly developed Carbon Contained Film (CCF). A film with highly efficient interfacial$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$consumption ability was identified. To distinguish the differences of the ability between the films, their water content and surface functional active sites were characterized. Additionally, investigation of the bonding interface mechanism revealed a unique C-rich layer, which consumes more interfacial water at low temperatures.

sources.title: Pure Ru n-TSV Processing and Extreme All-Dry SOI Wafer Thinning for a Backside Power-Delivery Network
sources.abstract: The backside power-delivery network (BSPDN) has emerged as a promising solution to address wiring congestion challenges in advanced nodes beyond the 3 nm technology threshold. In this study, we demonstrate a novel ruthenium (Ru)-based nano through-silicon via (n-TSV) interconnection technology fabricated on a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrate for BSPDN implementation. After fabricating a scallop-free n-TSV array with a high aspect ratio (AR) (10.4:1.0) using an advanced multi-step etching process, pure Ru metallization was achieved with a resistivity of 19.9 μΩ·cm. The double-side interconnection adopts a combination of an extreme wafer-thinning technique (final thickness: 500 nm; total thickness variation (TTV): < 15 nm) and a plasma-assisted all-dry revealing process, achieving high-precision n-TSV exposure from the backside of the substrate while preserving sidewall dielectric liner integrity (< 1 nm loss). A dry recess etch of Ru in n-TSVs was first developed, with significant selectivity (Ru-to-liner oxide ratio > 50:1), effectively eliminating the metallic sidewall residues. The further extracted average line resistance of the Ru-filled n-TSVs was as low as 29 Ω·μm −1 . Finally, after 100 thermal cycling tests (–40 to 125 °C), the relative resistance change remained below 1%, demonstrating the superior reliability and stability of the Ru-based interconnects in the BSPDN. These advancements establish a robust interconnection solution for achieving energy-efficient three-dimensional integrated circuit architectures.

sources.title: In-situ Co-Integration of Ru-based Buried Power Rails and nTSVs for Advanced Backside Power Delivery
sources.abstract: ABSTRACT The relentless scaling of semiconductor technology necessitates transformative solutions for power delivery networks (PDNs). Backside PDNs have emerged as a promising approach by decoupling power and signal interconnects. However, the integration of key components like buried power rails (BPRs) and nano-through-silicon vias (nTSVs) faces significant challenges, including interfacial instability and stringent alignment requirements. This work introduces a robust integration strategy utilizing Ruthenium (Ru) as the fill material for both BPRs and nTSVs, leveraging its superior chemical stability. An in-situ co-integration scheme is demonstrated, featuring a self-aligned etching process that enables the precise formation of nTSVs directly onto the BPRs, eliminating critical overlay constraints. An atomic layer deposition process achieves simultaneous, void-free, and conformal Ru metallization without a separate diffusion barrier. Furthermore, an innovative ion-beam thinning-back process is successfully implemented for the precise recess of Ru, overcoming the polishing challenges associated with this hard metal. Electrical characterization reveals an excellent and consistent line resistance of 11.4-11.8 Ω/μm for the co-integrated interconnects. The electromigration performance is rigorously assessed, and a comprehensive multiphysics model is established, showing strong agreement between experimental and simulated failure times, thereby validating its predictive accuracy. This work provides a holistic solution that paves the way for high-performance and highly reliable backside PDNs in advanced 3D integrated circuits (ICs).

findings.rationale: Two independent simulation studies (phase-field and electro-thermal-stress coupled) flag EM. One reports agreement with experiments, the other is simulation only. Both are abstract-only, so the magnitude of the risk at production conditions is not visible. Neither abstract gives absolute lifetimes.

findings.rationale: Single simulation-framework paper. The abstract quotes two different figures, a factor of 2 to 4 and 15%-25%, and does not explain how they differ (probably different metrics). A separate TSV experiment measured equivalent stress below 100 MPa for 1-4 µm TSVs. That is a narrow test on test structures, not a full BSPDN die in a package, so the two results do not directly contradict each other. Package-level validation is a gap.

findings.claim: Wafer-level manufacturing steps unique to BSPDN (extreme wafer thinning, direct bonding, hard-metal planarization, tight alignment) are still being solved at lab scale. Yield and cost at volume are not shown in these abstracts.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstracts describe new processes developed to address problems: interfacial water that harms bonding reliability, polishing difficulty with Ru, and stringent alignment needs. Demonstrations are small test structures, such as 500 nm thinning on SOI, 100 thermal cycles, or a first experimental demonstration. No defect density, throughput or cost data appear. This is a gap in evidence, not proof of failure. Interpretation is across papers, and the abstracts do not say whether the problems are resolved at HVM scale.

findings.claim: Reliability and integration solutions increasingly depend on a shift to ruthenium for rails and nTSVs. This adds materials-process maturity risk (hard-to-polish metal, new etch and recess processes) and concentration risk on a single metal option.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Simulations point to Ru-BPR as the most important factor in EM time to failure. The experimental papers build Ru structures with new process steps (all-dry thinning, ion-beam recess, self-aligned etch). The abstracts do not compare against W or Mo experimentally or report Ru supply or cost data. The timing is my judgement, not stated in the abstracts.

findings.claim: The strongest positive silicon evidence for HVM-style backside power comes from a single vendor (Intel), in its own papers. Independent replication and data on other foundries' processes are absent from this set.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both papers present vendor-reported results from a test chip (an E-core on Intel 4 finFET). The 2024 paper also dismisses some concerns as 'perceived' challenges. Results come from a single design and a single process, so generalization to other designs or processes is unproven. Other papers in the set are academic or consortium research without comparable production silicon.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Silicon results from an X-86 Intel E-Core test-chip validating PowerVia benefits are detailed.

findings.claim: Debug, failure analysis and characterization of backside power networks are harder because internal metal layers are not accessible with traditional probing. This adds cost and risk to bring-up and yield learning.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single abstract, with the problem statement stronger than the evidence. The proposed e-beam solution is described in promotional terms, and the abstract contains no measured results. Cited by 0 papers. Whether e-beam probing is practical in production is a gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: However, the characterization and debugging of these structures remain significant challenges due to the inaccessibility of internal metal layers when using traditional probing techniques.

findings.claim: Thermal behavior of BSPDN at chip and system level is under-evidenced. Thermal issues are named as concerns and hotspots are assessed only for particular configurations, but no full-chip or package-level thermal measurements appear.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: One paper calls thermal and reliability 'important concerns'. The other assesses thermal aspects (chip versus transistor level) for various configurations without giving numbers in the abstract. This is a gap in the retrieved evidence, not a demonstrated failure.

hype_flags: 'Game changer' / 'revolutionary' framing (e.g. src_f77c600510, src_17ef885673): the abstracts show lab demonstrations or proposals and give no volume yield or cost evidence.
'The rest of the silicon industry is racing to deploy' (src_17946b970d): an assertion by a vendor-authored paper, with no supporting data on other foundries.
'Perceived' challenges (src_17946b970d): downplays real reliability, thermal and mechanical issues raised in simulation papers.
'Robust integration solution' (src_a5cfab6d14, src_f6d4f33c8c): based on small test structures and limited stress tests (e.g. 100 thermal cycles).

finding.claim: S3 says thermal management is 'repeatedly identified as the principal drawback' of BSPD. The cited abstracts support only that thermal is one concern. One cited paper (src_7762759087) finds parasitic effects, not self-heating, dominate circuit dynamic performance. Another (src_925a2367d1) is a transient thermal-modelling workflow with no comparison of drawbacks. 'Principal' is not supported, and the thermal evidence is modelling-based. Electromigration, mechanical stress and process risks are also documented.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This cited paper ranks parasitic effects above self-heating for circuit performance, which cuts against calling thermal the principal drawback. Only src_a91300a32b states the increased thermal-resistance mechanism, and it does so within an FEA modelling study. The workflow paper src_925a2367d1 does not rank drawbacks, so it does not support 'principal'. Ranking drawbacks would need cross-comparison evidence that is not in the cited abstracts.
finding.supporting_excerpt: parasitic effects dominate circuit dynamic performance compared to self-heating effects (SHEs)

finding.claim: S4 says backside clock meshes 'consistently outperform' frontside meshes and calls the result 'verified'. The result comes from a single preprint and is simulation-only, using OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology, with SPICE checks. No silicon data is cited. 'Verified' means only that SPICE checked the design points. The average gains also depend on the authors' choice of 'identical' frontside mesh baseline and on four benchmarks.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is preprint, pre-silicon evidence from one academic technology model. 'Consistently' holds only over four designs. The finding should be framed as a simulated design-space result, not an established outcome. The preprint is also not independently corroborated in the set.
finding.supporting_excerpt: implemented in OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology. Four benchmarks (1,938 to 15,311 flip-flops) are explored

finding.claim: S2 and S12 rest the electrical benefits of BSPD on one vendor's own paper. The 30% droop and 6% frequency gains are measured against 'a similar design', not an identical one. They come from Intel's E-core on Intel 4 finFET. No independent replication or other-foundry data is in the set. S12's claim that the field has moved 'from demonstrating' benefits overstates how broadly they have been demonstrated.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The baseline is described as only 'similar', so design differences may contribute to the delta. Both cited silicon-evidence abstracts are Intel-authored (src_17946b970d speaks of Intel's 'E-Core test-chip validating PowerVia benefits'). The numbers should be read as vendor-reported, single-source, and specific to one finFET implementation, not generalised to RibbonFET or other processes.
finding.supporting_excerpt: compared to a similar design without PowerVia

finding.claim: S12 lists integration and thermal side-effects but omits reliability risks that the evidence set documents. These include electromigration in buried rails and nTSVs, self-heating-coupled degradation, and stress and delamination around µTSVs. It also omits the dependence of several solutions on ruthenium. As a summary of where the field is heading, the finding is incomplete and reads more favourably than the evidence.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Reliability is a distinct problem class. The EM abstracts show time to failure depends on rail metal and grain structure. The cross-layer paper reports that omitting self-heating underestimates degradation by 2 to 4 times. The mechanical paper reports delamination risk. None appear in S12's list of side-effects.

finding.claim: S9 presents embedded microfluidic cooling with BSPD as a way to use backside area for both power and heat. Both cited papers are modelling or FEA studies, and one uses the hedged wording 'can potentially offer'. No fabricated device or measured cooling benefit is cited. The finding also ignores that microchannels would compete with the already-limited backside routing and thinning budget.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts describe proposals and simulations (FEA, homogenization models), not demonstrated hardware. The finding should be labelled a conceptual, simulation-stage mitigation. The manufacturing feasibility and trade-off with backside routing resources are not addressed in the abstracts.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We propose a synergistic integration of microfluidic channels with power delivery on the backside of semiconductor dies that can potentially offer optimized space utilization

finding.claim: S5 says co-optimization frameworks are 'being proposed' that balance IR-drop, congestion and PPA and mitigate signal-integrity loss. This rests on one preprint whose gains are the authors' own experimental claim. The abstract gives no benchmark scale, technology basis or silicon validation. The SI result also depends on the framework's own models.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is a single-source preprint with only an abstract available. The plural 'frameworks' in the finding is not supported by the cited evidence, which contains one framework. The claim of SI mitigation is the authors' assertion and is not independently checked.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Experiments demonstrate improved WNS/TNS, frequency, and SI robustness without additional shielding overhead.

limitations: Only titles and abstracts of 12 papers were available, so methods, error bars and caveats in the full texts were not examined.

All retrieved papers are from OpenAlex. Several are conference papers, and no peer-review status was verified. Many risk statements rest on simulations (EM, self-heating, stress) without full silicon validation.
No papers cover cost, yield economics, supply chain, EDA maturity or competing approaches (e.g. improved frontside power delivery), so these risks are gaps in coverage, not findings.
The evidence is narrow: heavy on EM, TSV and process steps, and light on system-level thermal, test-chip scale and non-Intel production data.
Search was risk-oriented and returned several mostly positive process papers, so the set may under-represent negative results.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were reviewed. Some abstracts are truncated, so full-paper caveats may exist that were not seen.
The evidence set is small (23 papers), and one paper (src_b1bae9c128) has no abstract, so its process-integration challenges could not be assessed.
Nearly all thermal, reliability and clock-mesh findings are simulation or modelling. Several are preprints with no citation history. This review cannot judge model quality.
I did not challenge S1, S6, S7, S8, S10 or S11. They appear consistent with their abstracts, though S10 is model-only.

draft.summary: Research and patent activity on backside power delivery is rising quickly: papers went from 48 to 77 between 2024 and 2025 and 2026 is still ahead of 2025 year to date, while patent publications rose from 111 to 168 over the same period [S1][P1]. The only commercial evidence is Intel's annual report, which says its 18A process introduces backside power delivery (PowerVia) in high-volume manufacturing and will be used for several generations of its own CPUs [M1][M2]. Beyond that, the electrical benefit data is single-vendor, and the cited papers focus on unresolved thermal, reliability, bonding and debug issues, so the evidence for a broad market is thin [S12][R6][C3][C4]. No filings in the retrieved set mention TSMC, Samsung or equipment makers on this topic, although their patent filings suggest competition [M4][P1]. Intel's share price has also fallen sharply and is highly volatile, which is risk context only [T1][T2]. The main uncertainty is whether the approach scales beyond one vendor at acceptable yield, cost and thermal behaviour. Research and patent counts are not proof of commercial success.
draft.plain_summary: Backside power delivery moves a chip's power wiring to the back of the silicon so the front is freed up for signals. Research papers and patent filings are growing fast, and Intel says it has put the technology into its latest manufacturing process. What could stop it is heat, reliability and difficult manufacturing steps, and so far most of the real-world evidence comes from just one company.

limitations: Science and Risk findings rely largely on abstracts, preprints and simulation studies, not verified production data.

Patent applications are claims, and recent patent counts are undercounted due to publication delay.
Research and patent counts are not normalised for general growth and are not proof of commercial success.
Price findings cover one stock over about 100 trading days and are risk context only, not a signal.

dimensions.label: Research Momentum
dimensions.rationale: Papers with the topic phrases rose from 48 (2024) to 77 (2025), +60%, and 2026 year to date is 85 vs 60 (+42%), so momentum is still building. The counts are not normalised for overall publishing growth, and research activity is not commercial success. Content points to a field moving to integration and thermal problems.

dimensions.label: Patent Momentum
dimensions.rationale: Patent publications rose from 111 (2024) to 168 (2025), +51%, with 155 already in 2026 despite publication delay. Filings span fine vias, GAA and 3D integration, AI power delivery, and supplier etching processes. Applications are claims, not proof.

dimensions.label: Technical Feasibility
dimensions.rationale: Intel states it uses backside power in a high-volume process, and nTSV flows have been demonstrated. Performance numbers come from one vendor's paper, thermal and reliability results are largely modelled, and wafer-level steps are still being solved at lab scale. Feasibility is shown for one vendor, not broadly.

dimensions.label: Commercial Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Intel's 10-K describes backside power as introduced in high-volume manufacturing on 18A and planned for several CPU generations. No yield, cost or revenue data is in the excerpts, and R4 notes that volume yield and cost are not shown.

dimensions.label: Customer Adoption
dimensions.rationale: The only adoption evidence is Intel's plan for its own CPU products. No external customers or other companies' filings mention the topic, so adoption beyond Intel is unevidenced.

dimensions.label: Industry Investment
dimensions.rationale: Intel commits 18A to several product generations, and TSMC, Samsung, IBM and suppliers such as Applied Materials file patents. Filings are not spending figures, and no capex or investment data for other firms is in the set.

dimensions.label: Competitive Position
dimensions.rationale: Intel claims an industry first in volume, but the evidence is its own statement, while TSMC, Samsung and IBM lead patent filings. Other foundries' product status is unknown, so relative position cannot be firmly judged.

dimensions.label: Supply-Chain Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Equipment and chemical suppliers are filing patents for backside-power processes, but extreme thinning, bonding and hard-metal planarization are still lab-scale, ruthenium adds maturity and concentration risk, and no tool-maker filings mention the topic.
